text:
Ontario

Supreme Court

Tanny v. Tanny,

Date: 2000-06-28

Sanda Tanny,
Plaintiff

and

David Tanny,
Defendant

Ontario
Superior Court of Justice Kiteley J.

Heard:
March 31, 2000

Judgment: June 28,
2000

Docket: 00-FA-8629
FIS

Maurice Vaturi, for Plaintiff.

Edwin A. Flak, for Defendant.

Kiteley J.:

[
1
]

This was a motion brought by the defendant, David Tanny seeking to
either dismiss or stay the action of the plaintiff, Sanda Tanny. The parties
will be referred to as the husband and the wife although they have been divorced.

Background

[
2
]

This case has a long, complicated history, the details of which I
have set out in an earlier decision reported at (1998),
1998 CanLII 29642 (ON CTGD)
, 36 R.F.L. (4th) 307
(Ont. Gen. Div.). For the purposes of this motion, only some of the background
proceedings need be repeated.

[
3
]

In 1994, the wife commenced a divorce action, in which she included
claims under the
Divorce Act
,
the
Family Law Act,
and the
Children’s
Law Reform Act.

[
4
]

In January, 1997, the defendant husband brought a motion seeking to
have the wife’s pleadings struck out pursuant to
section 21.1
of the
Divorce
Act

and section 2(6) of the
Family Law Act,
on account
of
her
failure to remove the barriers to remarriage by consenting to receive the Get.
The Get is a divorce granted by a Rabbinical Court. It is a release from the religious bonds of marriage that must be
obtained before a Jewish spouse can remarry according to and in the Jewish
faith. The Rabbinical Court may
only grant the Get with the consent of the non-requesting party. In June, 1997,
Ferrier J. made an order requiring the wife to “forthwith take all necessary
steps required by her, to remove the religious barriers to each of the parties’
religious remarriages”. The motion came on again and by order dated August 26, 1997, Walsh J. made the following
order:

1. This Court Orders that, pursuant to
section 21.1

of the
Divorce Act
and section 2(6) of the Family Law Act, the
Petitioner’s proceeding shall be and is hereby dismissed.

2. This Court Orders that the Petitioner’s
pleadings, affidavits and financial statements shall be and are hereby struck
out.

The wife did not appeal that order.

[
5
]

The husband then brought a motion for an order permitting him to
file an Amended Answer and Counterpetition, and an order that all interim
orders were of no force and effect, and an order prohibiting the wife from
pleading to the Amended Answer and Counterpetition. The wife was served with
that motion record on September 5th. She did not attend the motion on September
9th nor was she represented. The materials presented to Walsh J. included
evidence that the Amended Answer and Counterpetition had been sent to the
wife’s counsel in April, 1997 and consequently, the wife was aware of the
contents. Walsh J. made the following order:

This Court Orders that, pursuant to the
Rules of Civil Procedure, the Respondent shall file an Amended Answer and
Counterpetition in the form sent to the Petitioner on April 23, 1997.

This Court Orders that, pursuant to the
Courts of Justice Act, all interim orders in this proceeding are of no force
and effect as at August 26, 1997.

This Court Orders that, pursuant to the
Courts of Justice Act and the Rules of Civil Procedure, the Petitioner shall be
and is hereby prohibited from pleading to the Amended Answer and
Counterpetition.

The wife made no effort until October, 1997 to
find out what had transpired and she did not appeal from that order.

[
6
]

At paragraphs 21-22 of the reported reasons, I outlined the events
surrounding the motion for summary judgment brought by the husband and the
order which I made on January 8, 1998. The wife consented to receipt of the Get
on January 15, 1998, although
she continues to deny that she acted freely and voluntarily. After she removed
the barriers, the wife brought a motion returnable on February 5, 1998 seeking
leave to file an Answer to the husband’s Amended Answer and Counterpetition. In
reasons dated February 16, 1998
(reported as indicated above) I gave the wife leave to file an Answer to the
Amended Answer and Counterpetition and imposed conditions for her continued
participation in the proceedings.

[
7
]

Two years later and with the assistance of recently engaged counsel,
the wife started this action by statement of claim. She seeks relief under the
Family
Law Act
similar to the relief requested in her original divorce petition
including child and spousal support and a claim for an unequal division of the
net family property in her favour, and additional claims including a claim for
occupation rent, and a claim under the Partition Act for sale of the matrimonial
home. The husband seeks a stay or dismissal of her action on the grounds that
her claims have already been dismissed.

Issues

[
8
]

This motion was approached from two different perspectives:

a) Is the wife barred from commencing a new
action based on principles of
res judicata
and/or issue estoppel?

b) what, if any, rights does a party regain
upon curing the conduct which originally caused the court to dismiss that
party’s claims?

Analysis

Issue 1: The Applicability of the
doctrines of Res Judicata/Issue Estoppel

[
9
]

Issue estoppel is a form of res judicata. The difference between
the two was outlined by the Ontario Court of Appeal in
McQuillan v Native
Inter-Tribal Housing Co-operative Inc.,
(unreported) November 27, 1998
[reported (1998),
1998 CanLII 6408 (ON CA)
, 20 R.P.R. (3d) 198 (Ont. C.A.)]. At paragraph 7, Charron J.A.
explained:

Simply put, res judicata or “cause of
action estoppel” precludes a person from bringing an action against another
when that same cause of action has been determined in earlier proceedings by a
court of competent jurisdiction. Issue estoppel will prevent a person from
relitigating a question where, the cause of action being different, the same
question was decided in a final judicial decision in earlier proceedings
between the same parties.

[
10
]

Issue estoppel is said to have three
requirements: the same question, or issue, has been decided, the judicial
decision said to create the estoppel is final, and the parties to the judicial
decision or their privies are the same parties to the proceeding in which the
issue estoppel is raised:
Angle v. Minister of National Revenue
(1974),

1974 CanLII 168 (SCC)
, [1975] 2 S.C.R. 248 (S.C.C.).

[
11
]

Res judicata
prohibits the re-litigation
of matters that have already been decided and requires that the parties put
forward their entire case in a single action. It reflects the fact that
litigation by installment is not tolerated:
Tsaoussis (Litigation Guardian
of
)
v. Baetz
(1998),
1998 CanLII 5454 (ON CA)
, 41 O.R. (3d) 257 (Ont. C.A.).
Res judicata
can also extend
to matters that ought to have been raised when the matter was first heard. It
applies not only to points upon which the court was actually required by the
parties to form an opinion and pronounce a judgment, but to every point which
properly belonged to the subject of litigation, and which the parties,
exercising reasonable diligence, might have brought forward at the time:
Maynard
v. Maynard
(1950),
1950 CanLII 3 (SCC)
, [1951] S.C.R. 346 (S.C.C.).

[
12
]

Mr. Flak argued the motion mainly in terms
of
res judicata
and issue estoppel, although he also submitted that the
action was an abuse of process, and an attempt to interfere with or sidestep
Walsh J.’s order. The crux of his position was that all of the claims in the
wife’s new statement of claim had already been adjudicated and dismissed in
Walsh J.’s order of August, 1997. He relied on paragraph 1 of the order dated
August 26, 1997 as set out above. Mr. Flak also argued that the statement
of claim in the new action was essentially identical to the dismissed petition
for divorce, and that any minor differences were still barred by
res
judicata,
since they could have been raised in the initial petition.

[
13
]

The key issue on the motion was whether a
dismissal pursuant to section 2(6) of the
Family Law Act
or
section 21.1

of the
Divorce Act

could properly be considered an adjudication on the
merits.

[
14
]

Mr. Flak submitted almost 20 authorities,
none of which dealt squarely with the question of whether a dismissal for the
failure to remove a religious bar to remarriage constituted adjudication on the
merits or could function to bar a second action. Most of the cases were
distinguished by Mr. Vaturi.

[
15
]

In my view, the most relevant case in
Mr. Flak’s materials was
Tsaoussis, supra.
In that case, a minor
plaintiff was involved in a car accident. The parties reached a settlement for
approximately $5000, which was approved by the court. After the funds were paid
into court, counsel for the defendant wrote a letter to the plaintiff’s
counsel, confirming that the payment resolved all claims arising out of the
incident. Subsequently, it was determined that the child plaintiff had numerous
ongoing medical and developmental problems stemming from the injuries she
suffered in the accident. The plaintiff retained new counsel, and commenced an
action for $2.2 million in damages. The defendant argued that the claim had
already been settled such that the plaintiff had no cause of action. The trial
judge allowed the new action to proceed on the basis that there was new medical
evidence, and that the original judgment could no longer be viewed as in the
best interests of the child. The Court of Appeal set aside the judgment and
dismissed the new action. Doherty J.A. emphasized the importance of finality in
litigation, and held that a judgment approving a settlement that has been
signed, entered and appealed is final, and must be given the same force as any
other final judgement. He held that any evidence which could reasonably have
been tendered prior to judgment could not be used to afford a party a second
opportunity to re-litigate the same issue.

[
16
]

Finality in litigation is the principle which
informs both
res judicata
and issue estoppel. When claims are resolved,
either through a trial, a settlement, or a dismissal of an action for
substantive reasons, both parties are barred from commencing the action again.
It is settled law that these doctrines bar the relitigation of questions and
causes of action that have already been adjudicated on the merits.

[
17
]

At the same time, it is settled law that a
judgment is not on the merits where it is based merely on rules of procedure.
For example, when an action is dismissed because the pleadings disclose no
cause of action, a second action is not prohibited. In
AGF Canadian Equity
Fund v. Transamerica Commercial Finance Corp.
Canada

(1993),
1993 CanLII 8682 (ON CTGD)
, 14 O.R. (3d) 161 (Ont. Gen.
Div.) Borins J. (as he then was) considered the consequences of a judgment of
the motions court judge dismissing the first action for failure to disclose a
reasonable cause of action because a material averment had been omitted. At
page 172-3, he referred to the “liberal amendment policy of the Rules of Civil
Procedure” which was based on the “policy that cases should be finally decided
on their merits and not on technicalities.” Borins J. concluded that a second
action was not barred based on this analysis at page 178:

…because the merits of a case have not been
dealt with the dismissal of an action because a material averment has been
omitted from the statement of claim does not constitute a bar to another action
arising out of the same circumstances and based on a a statement from the first
action. Viewed in a functional sense, as the effect of the original motion was
not to consider the merits of the plaintiffs’ claims it follows that the effect
of the judgment was not an adjudication of the merits of those claims. Stated
differently, the defendants’ position is based on the form of the judgment when
it is the substance of the matter actually decided which should control.

[
18
]

For purposes of this motion, I need not find
that the dismissal of an action due to a refusal to remove the barriers to
remarriage is equivalent to a dismissal based on procedural rules or legal
technicalities. The fact remains that Walsh J. never considered the merits of
the wife’s claims. He merely considered whether she was refusing to remove the
barriers to the remarriage of the husband. Her petition for divorce (and the
claims for corollary relief) was dismissed for failing to remove those
barriers. I find that the claims made by the wife have never been adjudicated
on the merits. I therefor conclude that the recent proceeding by the wife is
not prohibited by the doctrines of
res judicata
or issue estoppel.

Issue
#2:
What
is the effect of the Wife having Cured the Conduct which gave rise to the order
dismissing her petition for divorce?

[
19
]

Mr. Vaturi took a different approach to
the motion. It was his position that the wife was entitled to participate in
litigation by commencing her action once she had cured her default. Before
turning to that analysis, I refer to the relevant sections:

Divorce Act

s.21.1(3) Where a spouse who has been
served with an affidavit under subsection (2) does not

(a) within fifteen days after that
affidavit is filed with the court or within such longer period as the court
allows, serve on the deponent and file with the court an affidavit indicating
that all of the barriers referred to in paragraph (2)(e) have been removed, and

(b) satisfy the court, in any additional
manner that the court may require, that all of the barriers referred to in
paragraph (2)(e) have been removed,

the court may, subject to any terms that
the court considers appropriate,

(c) dismiss any application filed by that
spouse under this Act, and

(d) strike out any other pleadings and
affidavits filed by that spouse under this Act.

Family Law Act:

s.2(5) Within ten days after service of the
statement, or within such longer period as the court allows, the party served
with a statement under subsection (4) shall serve on the other party and
file with the court a statement, verified by oath or statutory declaration,
indicating that the author of the statement has removed all barriers that are
within his or her control and that would prevent the other spouse’s remarriage
within that spouse’s faith.

s.2(6) When a party fails to comply with
subsection (5),

(a) if the party is an applicant, the
proceeding may be dismissed;

(b) if the party is a respondent, the
defence may be struck out.

[
20
]

Mr. Vaturi anchored his submissions on an
analysis of the purpose of the two sections, and focused on the extent to which
they should impact on a spouse’s rights in the long term. It was his position
that these sections were enacted as tools that would facilitate divorces
by imposing consequences on litigants who failed to remove barriers to
remarriage. He rejected the idea that the provisions were intended to be
punitive, or to deprive spouses of their matrimonial rights forever.

[
21
]

Mr. Vaturi submitted that once the
withholding party agreed to receive the Get, the tools have served their
purpose, and the substantive claims should be allowed to proceed. He recognized
that the wife could not avoid the consequences of my order dated February 16, 1998, or the original order of Walsh
J., but submitted that there was nothing preventing her from commencing a new
action. He urged me to interpret the sections liberally, in order to
achieve a just result. He rejected the idea that the wife could be regarded as
abusing the legal process simply by seeking to exercise her inherent rights.
Mr. Vaturi submitted that the statutes only contemplate eliminating the
withholding spouse’s right to participate in the proceedings until he or she
complies with the provision, not forever.

[
22
]

There are few Canadian cases dealing with the
provincial or
Divorce Act

provisions concerning the failure to remove
religious barriers to re-marriage. In what appears to be the first reported
decision under the Divorce Act, in
Glass v. Glass
(February 23, 1987),
Doc. D120917/84 (Ont. Master), Master Cork made an order requiring the wife to
give her irrevocable consent to the Get within 30 days of the husband setting
down the divorce for trial. In 1993 in
Rokach v. Rokach,
unreported,
Epstein J. made an order that all of the proceedings were stayed until the
religious barriers to remarriage were removed. In 1995 in
Levy v. Levy,
unreported,
Jennings J. made an order requiring the husband to obtain a Get in Toronto acceptable to the wife within eight
months. The order indicates that it was on consent.

[
23
]

S. (E.) v. S. (O.)
(October 6, 1995),
Doc. C.S. Montréal 500-12-221804-952 (Que. S.C.) was decided under
section 21.1

of the
Divorce Act
,
and provides some useful discussion of the purpose
of that section. In that case, the wife sought a dismissal of the husband’s
petition for divorce, on the grounds that the husband refused to grant his
consent to the Get. Tannebaum J. held that the husband’s refusal was
unjustified, and dismissed the husband’s petition for divorce.

[
24
]

Tannenbaum J. outlined the implications of the
Get, and the purpose of the provisions. He noted that since the granting of the
Get requires the consent of the non-requesting party, men have historically
used the threat of withholding consent to force women into accepting unfair
agreements with respect to their matrimonial claims. Tannenbaum J. viewed
section 21.1

as a way to level the playing field for divorcing people of the Jewish faith.
The party withholding consent can be denied the right to petition for corollary
relief or even a civil divorce itself. He further held that the section clearly
indicates that the barriers are to be removed prior to the completion of civil
proceedings, since it empowers the court to dismiss any proceedings brought by
the refusing spouse. Tannenbaum J. granted the motion by the wife and dismissed
the petition for divorce which had been issued on behalf of the husband.

[
25
]

Tannenbaum J. also indirectly shed light on the
question of whether 21.1 should be interpreted as permanently barring the
claims of the refusing party. In the context of dismissing the husband’s
petition for divorce, he noted that “agreeing to the Ghet prior to completion
of the civil divorce would in no way prevent the husband from continuing with
his proceedings, including his request for custody…” I infer from that passage
that a petitioner may have the petition dismissed for failure to remove the
barriers to remarriage, but may subsequently become re-involved in litigation
after removing the barriers to remarriage by consenting to the Get. I note that
Tannenbaum J. did not make any comments suggesting that the dismissal of the
petition would bar any subsequent petition.

[
26
]

The husband in
S. (E.) v. S. (O.)
also
brought an action in separation claiming financial matters, custody and a
proceeding for habeas corpus. The wife brought motions to dismiss the husband’s
proceedings. The second reported reasons (December 19, 1996),
Doc. C.S. Montréal 500-04-004226-958 (Que. S.C.) arose from a motion
to decline jurisdiction of the court on certain matters concerning the custody
of a child because the husband had filed a “request for return” with the
Central Authority of Quebec seeking the return of the child who was then living
in Israel. The court declined jurisdiction. The reasons include reference to
the earlier decision of Tannenbaum J. But it is not clear from the reasons for
decision the extent to which the refusal by the husband to remove the barriers
to remarriage had an impact on the outcome.

[
27
]

Mr. Vaturi relied on
S. (E.) v. S. (O.)

for support for the proposition that the husband was allowed to institute
another action in the same court notwithstanding the dismissal of his divorce
pursuant to
section 21.1
. On Mr. Flak’s careful reading, the Hague
Convention action had been started prior to the divorce action and had not been
included when the wife had brought the motion to dismiss which was heard by
Tannenbaum J. Mr. Flak asserted that the second decision in
S. (E.) v.
S. (O.)
may have also been affected by specified sections of the

Quebec Civil Code
. Mr. Flak pointed out that it is speculative as to why
the court declined jurisdiction on all matters before it since no reasons for
were given. I agree with Mr. Flak on the absence of reasons.

[
28
]

Mr. Flak identified the distinction
between the Family Law Act and the
Divorce Act
in that the latter statute
provides the court with greater latitude in the making of its orders. However,
the order made by Walsh J. in August, 1997 was expressly pursuant to both
sections. Consequently, the distinction here is less material. The wife has
brought her proceeding under the provincial legislation and, in that respect,
it might be said that the more restrictive section applies. I will address
that issue below.

[
29
]

Mr. Flak pointed out that the provisions in
both statutes were substantially or almost exclusively authored by John Syrtash
whose efforts were supported by Jewish organizations. The legislation was
passed at both levels without opposition. Mr. Flak referred to what he
described as a “seminal article and text” by Mr. Syrtash namely:
Removing
Barriers to Religious Remarriage in Ontario; Rights and Remedies
(1987) 1
C.F.L.Q. 310 and
Religion and Culture in Canadian Family Law,
Butterworths,
Toronto (1992). Mr. Flak
submitted that the basic policy reasons behind the passage of the legislation
are set out at page 328 of Mr. Syrtash’s articles as follows:

The policy reasoning behind the section 2
legislation as expressed in the Justice Committee debates is not the secular
enforcement of a religious procedure, but is precisely to prevent the abuse of
a contractual release in Jewish marital relations from interfering in the civil
and secular rights of an economically-disadvantaged spouse. Moreover, the
victim’s religious freedom is gravely compromised when she is obliged to choose
between insisting on her civil or property rights under the Act or adhering to
the tenets of her faith as they pertain to remarriage. The remedial purpose of
such legislation is to relieve such a person from making a ridiculous choice.

[
30
]

Mr. Vaturi agrees with that statement as
the policy upon which the legislators acted. Consequently, I need not address
whether policy can be enumerated for the court by reference to the publications
of the proponent of the legislation.

[
31
]

Where Mr. Vaturi and Mr. Flak part
company is whether a spouse who fails to remove barriers to remarriage is able
to recover the right to pursue claims once the barriers have been removed. Most
of the original oral and written submissions were made by Mr. Vaturi and
Mr. Flak on the basis of the estoppel principles. At the conclusion of
those submissions, I asked both counsel to undertake further investigations to
determine whether the issue of regaining rights to litigate under the
Divorce
Act
or the Family Law Act had been canvassed by any other court. I directed
both counsel to be brief. Neither counsel followed that direction. However,
since I was interested in any assistance which could be found in the
authorities, I have overlooked the lack of brevity.

[
32
]

In early May, Mr. Vaturi forwarded a brief
which included further written submissions, the head-note of a decision in the
Supreme Court of Canada and a reference to the dissenting reasons on the issue
of statutory interpretation, a letter of opinion from Mr. John Syrtash, a
letter of opinion from Ms. Judith Holzman (who was engaged with
Mr. Syrtash in the development of the statutory amendments) and the full
transcript of the hearing before Ferrier J. in August 1997. Mr. Flak
responded with a fullsome written submission, copies of reasons for decision in
two cases by the Ontario Court of Appeal, and the full text of the decision in
the Supreme Court of Canada to which reference was made by Mr. Vaturi.
Mr. Flak took exception to the introduction of opinion evidence in the
written submissions. At first review, I thought it inappropriate for
Mr. Flak to so critically challenge the opinion rendered by
Mr. Syrtash when Mr. Flak relied on his publications in his original
submissions. However, I ultimately concluded that Mr. Flak’s opposition to
the opinion evidence was well founded. I had asked counsel for brief
submissions to assist the court on the issue of regaining the right to
litigate. That was not an invitation to bolster the previous written and oral
submissions with material such as opinion letters to which Mr. Flak could
not adequately nor fairly respond. Accordingly, I place no reliance on the
opinions expressed by Mr. Syrtash and Ms. Holzman on the issue as to
whether a litigant who removes barriers to remarriage is entitled to
reinstatement.

[
33
]

Leaving that aside, in his written submissions,
Mr. Flak reiterated the unfairness to the husband if the wife is now
allowed to pick up where she left off. Mr. Flak has taken some liberties
in his submissions in that they are not wholly supported by the evidence, but
he asserted that the husband could never be restored to the position he was in
prior to the wife’s recalcitrant behaviour. He cited the legal fees associated
with the Get related aspect of the case, the unpaid award of costs by Walsh J.,
the compounding of the husband’s estrangement with his daughter, and the
exacerbation of his health problems if compensable at all. He pointed out that
the husband has the “right” to rely on orders that have been made and that he
ought to be protected from abuses.

[
34
]

Provisions dealing with the refusal to remove
religious barriers are unique in the sense that they deal with conduct
outside

the lawsuit. It is the failure of a spouse to do something which has no
relation to his or her actual claim which bars him or her from proceeding with
that claim.

[
35
]

It is helpful to consider the provisions by
analogizing to rules that deal with “bad conduct”
within
the lawsuit.
For example, in a situation where a party fails to file a defence, this can be
cured and the party can get back into the action. If a party fails to comply
with an order, this is also almost always relievable. Even if a party engages
in some kind of contemptuous behaviour which causes the pleadings to be struck
out, there is usually some potential relief, albeit on terms. These examples
highlight the fact that courts are hesitant to extinguish rights permanently
for inappropriate behavior. Although cost consequences may very well be leveled
against parties who engage in inappropriate litigation behaviour, courts
generally do not punish these litigants by denying them their day in court.

[
36
]

In light of this, it is difficult to
rationalize why a party who engages in “bad conduct” completely
outside
the
lawsuit should be shut out of the litigation forever. In my view, it is logical
to interpret the sections of the Family Law Act and the
Divorce Act
as
temporary bars to litigation. After a withholding party has cured the conduct
by removing the barriers to remarriage, he or she is free to commence a new
action. [I leave for another day whether there is relief available in a motion
brought pursuant to
s.21.1
or s.2 in the action which had been the subject of
the dismissal order.]

[
37
]

In arriving at a conclusion, it is important to
consider principles of statutory interpretation. In
Pointe-Claire (Ville) c.
S.E.P.B., Local 57,
1997 CanLII 390 (SCC)
, [1997] 1 S.C.R. 1015 (S.C.C.), the Supreme Court of
Canada dismissed an appeal in an administrative law matter. L’Heureux-Dube J.
wrote dissenting reasons. She referred to such principles. For purposes of this
case, it matters not that she wrote in dissent. The majority did not take issue
with the passage or the subject matter to which I will refer. In any event, I
adopt the following passage as an easy reference to unchallenged propositions.
With reference to
Driedger on the Construction of Statutes
(3rd ed.
1994) by R. Sullivan, at p. 131:

There is only one rule in modern
interpretation, namely, courts are obliged to determine the meaning of
legislation in its total context, having regard to the purpose of legislation,
the consequences of proposed interpretations, the presumptions and special
rules of interpretation, as well as admissible external aids. In other words,
the courts must consider and take into account all relevant and admissible
indicators of legislative meaning. After taking these into account, the court
must then adopt an interpretation that is appropriate. An appropriate
interpretation is one that can be justified in terms of (a) its plausibility,
that is, its compliance with the legislative text; (b) its efficacy, that is,
it’s promotion of the legislative purpose; and (c) its acceptability, that is,
the outcome is reasonable and just.

In the case at bar, the relevant aspects of
the modern rule are as follows: courts determine the meaning of legislation
having regard to the consequences of proposed interpretations, and the
presumptions of interpretation. After taking these into account, courts must
then adopt an interpretation that is appropriate in terms of its acceptability,
that is, the reasonableness of its outcome. One such presumption of
interpretation is the presumption against absurdity, which was codified as
follows in R.A.R. Bennion,
Statutory Interpretation: A Code
(2nd ed.
1992), at p.679:

Section 312. Presumption that absurd
result not intended

(1) The court seeks to avoid a construction
that produces an absurd result,… [including] virtually any result which is
unworkable or impracticable, inconvenient, anomalous or illogical, futile or
pointless, artificial, or productive of a disproportionate counter-mischief.

[
38
]

Applying those principles to this case leads me
to these conclusions. There is no question that the
Divorce Act
provision gives
rise to more discretion than in the Family Law Act. But a close review of the
entire section indicates that there is considerable latitude in both
statutes. Neither addresses expressly the prospect of an order for dismissal
and an order for reinstatement or substitute legal proceedings upon compliance.
But both contemplate the imposition of terms and/or the exercise of discretion:
in s. 2(5), 2(6), 2(8); and in s.21.1(3) and (4). I find that it is
plausible

to interpret both s.2 and
s.21.1
so as to permit a party who has been the
subject of a dismissal order to commence proceedings for relief similar to that
claimed in the proceedings which were dismissed after the barriers to
remarriage have been removed. I find that the
efficacy
of the
legislation is respected in that the barriers have been removed. And,
notwithstanding the assertions by Mr. Flak on behalf of the husband, I
find that it is
acceptable
to interpret the legislation to achieve that outcome.
It follows that I find that the outcome is reasonable and is not absurd.

[
39
]

I find that it would not be consistent with the
policy considerations informing the sections to interpret them in a way
which prohibits a party whose claims have been dismissed from ever having his
or her claims adjudicated on the merits. Upon curing the conduct which caused
the action to be dismissed, a party must be entitled to seek to have those
claims adjudicated. Both sections must be interpreted only as temporary
bars to participation in litigation.

[
40
]

The motion by the husband to stay the
proceeding on the basis that the wife is prohibited from starting an action as
a result of the order of Walsh J. dated August 26, 1997 is dismissed

[
41
]

Having said that, I have discretion to impose
terms on the wife which address the consequences to the husband of the refusal
by the wife to remove the barriers to remarriage. Mr. Flak’s submissions
were focussed on resisting the proceeding in its entirety. Having made the
decision that the action will not be dismissed, I invite both counsel to make
submissions as to the conditions which ought to be imposed. The husband has not
been successful in the motion. But given the circumstances under which this
matter came to be litigated, I see no circumstances which warrant an order in
favour of the wife for costs of this motion. With respect to costs
of the
motion,
the only issue will be whether the husband is entitled to costs.
Regardless of that issue, I expect counsel to make submissions as to the costs
incurred by the husband as a result of the refusal by the wife to remove the
barriers to remarriage.
